extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in mathematics and aesthetics (mathematicians and lay audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and characterizing what makes a mathematical formulation or result be experienced as 'beautiful,' drawing on aesthetic theory and neuroscience evidence. The page lists principles that can serve as evaluation criteria for mathematical elegance and aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: "The best mathematical formulations are usually those that are the most beautiful." Mathematicians value formulations described as "unexpected," "elegant," and "simple."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a formulation reduces complexity, reveals a concise expression, or unifies disparate ideas into a simple, elegant statement. Look for unexpected simplicity and economy of expression as positive marks; verbosity, unnecessary complication, or ad hoc constructions are negative signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic responses emerge from "identifying simplicity in complexity, pattern in chaos, structure in stasis."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree to which a result or proof exposes patterns, regularities, or recurring structure that were previously hidden. Reward clarity that makes complex phenomena appear organized; penalize presentations that obscure or fail to reveal underlying pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of form and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical beauty involves "balancing form and content, syntax and semantics, utility and autonomy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge both the formal (syntactic) neatness and the substantive (semantic) significance. A beautiful result harmonizes rigorous form with meaningful content and, where relevant, practical utility without sacrificing intrinsic elegance. Overemphasis on mere formalism or on raw applicability alone reduces perceived beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Poincaré: "the harmony of numbers and forms, of geometric elegance" produces "a true esthetic feeling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for harmonious relations among mathematical objects, coherence of structure, and symmetries that create a unified aesthetic impression. Disjointed arguments or disparate parts lacking structural unity detract from harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal resonance (neural correlates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neuroscience: "beautiful formulas stimulated activity in same field… as other researchers have identified as the seat of experience of beauty from other sources" — math beauty activates the same brain regions as artistic beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat aesthetic responses to mathematics as having measurable, cross-domain neural correlates. This supports comparing mathematical beauty to other aesthetic domains and suggests that criteria capturing what generally elicits aesthetic neural responses (e.g., symmetry, simplicity, surprise) are relevant. Use empirical findings to justify objective-seeming rubric elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Santayana, beauty emerges when mathematical symbols carry intrinsic worth and "attracts like a magnet all the values of things it is known to symbolize."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the expressive power of notation, concepts, and formulations: do symbols and statements encapsulate and evoke rich meaning beyond their literal form? Prefer formulations that convey insight and connect to broader values or concepts; avoid notation or presentation that is opaque or devoid of evocative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric-design implication: borrow from aesthetic theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Implication stated on the page: Beauty in math is not metaphorical — it is the same neural response as beauty in art. Rubric design can borrow from aesthetic theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing evaluation rubrics for mathematical work, incorporate dimensions from aesthetic theory (simplicity, harmony, expressiveness, pattern revelation, balance) and, where possible, link them to observable effects (clarity, unification, explanatory power, neural/psychological evidence). This entry functions as meta-guidance for designing assessment criteria rather than as a criterion of a single mathematical result.
